items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.

items.title: Plants can push water up — but only a few metres
items.claim: Roots actively pump ions into the xylem at night. Water follows by osmosis, generating pressure that pushes sap upward. You can see it as guttation: droplets of liquid forced out at leaf tips in the morning.
items.prompt: Why does root pressure not lift water all the way to a redwood canopy?

options.text: Root pressure rarely exceeds ~0.2 MPa — enough to push water ~20 metres. Taller transport requires transpiration-driven tension at the leaves (cohesion-tension theory)
Water cannot move upward in plants

items.reveal:
Two mechanisms drive xylem flow:

1. Root pressure (positive): active ion transport into xylem; water follows; positive pressure pushes sap upward. Works in small herbaceous plants, in young growing tissue, and in trees in early spring before leaves open. Maxes out at ~0.2 MPa.

2. Transpiration pull (tension, cohesion-tension theory): evaporation at leaves creates negative pressure; cohesive water column transmits the pull down to roots. Routinely reaches -1 to -2 MPa. Works in any tree height up to ~130 m.

Guttation is visible evidence of root pressure: drops of xylem sap forced out of hydathodes on leaf tips overnight (when stomata are closed and transpiration cannot relieve the pressure). Looks like dew but contains dissolved minerals.

Most mature trees rely entirely on transpiration pull. Root pressure becomes detectable only when transpiration is suppressed (humid nights, plant chopped down, etc.).

Notably, mosses lack vascular tissue entirely and rely on diffusion and capillary action — which is why they top out at ~20 cm.
items.why: Roots seem like obvious pumps. They are — but only weak ones. The real heavy lifting in tall plants is done by evaporation at the top, pulling on water held together by hydrogen bonds.
